baseProblem.statement: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated characters.

rounds.question: What state tracks the current no-repeat window?

options.rationale: A length alone can't tell you WHERE the window starts, so you can't shrink it when a repeat appears.

options.conceptLabel: Last-seen index per char, window start, and best

fragments.java: Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>(); int start = 0; int best = 0;

options.rationale: The last-seen map lets you jump the window start past a repeat in O(1), while best records the longest valid window.

options.conceptLabel: A set of characters in the window

fragments.java: Set<Character> window = new HashSet<>(); int start = 0; int best = 0;

options.rationale: A set works for a sliding window, but you must then shrink one character at a time; storing last-seen indices lets you jump directly.

options.conceptLabel: A frequency count of the whole string

fragments.python:
from collections import Counter
    counts = Counter(s)

options.rationale: A global frequency table describes the entire string, not a moving window, and never reveals repeats within a range.

rounds.question: With the last-seen map, window start, and best ready, how do you scan the string?

options.rationale: You need the index both to measure window length and to record each character's last-seen position.
Without the index you can't compute the window length i - start + 1 or store positions.

fragments.python:
for i in range(len(s)):
            for j in range(i, len(s)):
fragments.java: for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) for (int j = i; j < s.length(); j++) {

options.rationale: Enumerating every substring is O(n^2) or worse; the sliding window does it in one pass.
Scanning backwards complicates the 'jump start past the last occurrence' logic for no benefit.

rounds.question: As you reach each character c at index i, how do you react when c repeats inside the window?

options.conceptLabel: Reset the window start to zero
options.rationale: Jumping start back to 0 reopens characters you already passed, breaking the no-repeat guarantee.
Moving start by one isn't enough — the previous occurrence may be far back; you must jump past it.

options.conceptLabel: Jump start past the previous occurrence, if it's inside the window

fragments.python:
if c in last and last[c] >= start:
            start = last[c] + 1

options.rationale: Moving start to last[c] + 1 evicts exactly the stale repeat; the 'inside the window' guard avoids dragging start backwards.
Wiping all positions forgets characters still in the window, so later repeats go undetected.

rounds.question: With the window start fixed, what do you record for c before measuring the window?

options.conceptLabel: Update best but don't store the position
options.rationale: Skipping last[c] = i means the next repeat of c can't be located, so the window won't shrink correctly.

options.conceptLabel: Store the last-seen position, then update best

fragments.python:
last[c] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
fragments.java: last.put(s.charAt(i), i); best = Math.max(best, i - start + 1);

options.rationale: Record where you saw c so a future repeat can jump the start, then update best with the current window length.
best is a maximum window length, not a running count; incrementing it ignores window shrinking.

options.conceptLabel: Assign best to the current window length
options.rationale: Assigning (not maxing) lets a later, shorter window overwrite a longer one already found.

rounds.question: When the scan finishes, what do you return?

options.rationale: best is the longest no-repeat window seen — the answer.
The last window isn't necessarily the longest; you must track the maximum.
That's the count of distinct characters in the whole string, not the longest window.
Only correct when the whole string has no repeats; in general it overstates the answer.
